html:
One database server eventually isn't enough: too many reads, too much data, or too much risk if it dies. There are two answers, and they solve different problems. Replication copies the same data to several machines. Sharding splits the data so each machine holds a part.

Replication: The Same Data, Several Times

The most common setup has one primary (also called leader) that takes all writes, and several replicas (followers) that receive a copy of every change.

          writes
app ───────────────► primary
  │                   │  │
  │ reads             ▼  ▼
  └──────────► replica  replica

What it gives you:

  • More read capacity: spread reads over the replicas.
  • Safety: if the primary dies, a replica is promoted and takes over.
  • Closer data: a replica in another region serves local users faster.

What it doesn't give you: more write capacity. Every write still goes through one primary.

Synchronous or Asynchronous

  • Synchronous: the primary waits until a replica confirms before answering "saved". No data is lost if the primary dies, but every write is slower, and a stuck replica blocks writes.
  • Asynchronous: the primary answers at once and sends the change afterward. Fast, but the last changes can be lost in a crash, and replicas are slightly behind.

Most setups are asynchronous, sometimes with one synchronous replica as a safe backup.

Replication Lag

With asynchronous replicas, a replica can be a few milliseconds, or in bad moments seconds, behind. That causes classic bugs:

  • A user edits their profile, the page reloads from a replica, and the old name shows. Fix: read your own writes from the primary for a short time after a change.
  • Two reads hit two replicas at different points, and data seems to go back in time. Fix: send a user's reads to the same replica.

Sharding: Splitting the Data

When the data or the writes don't fit on one primary, you shard (or partition): each shard is a separate database holding some of the rows.

user_id 1–1M   ─► shard A
user_id 1M–2M  ─► shard B
user_id 2M–3M  ─► shard C

Each shard takes only its part of the writes and storage, so capacity grows with the number of shards. Each shard is usually replicated too.

Choosing the Shard Key

The shard key decides where each row goes. It's the most important decision, and hard to change later.

  • Range-based (user IDs 1–1M on shard A…): easy range queries, but new users all land on the last shard, a hot shard.
  • Hash-based (hash of the user ID, modulo the number of shards): spreads load evenly, but range queries must ask every shard.
  • Consistent hashing places shards on a ring, so adding a shard moves only a small part of the data instead of almost all of it.

A good shard key:

  • spreads writes evenly, with no single huge customer or celebrity on one shard,
  • keeps data read together on the same shard, like all of a user's orders under the user ID.

What Sharding Makes Hard

  • Queries across shards: "top 10 products of all users" must ask every shard and merge the results.
  • Joins across shards: usually done in the application, or avoided by keeping related data together.
  • Transactions across shards: need distributed transactions, or a design that avoids them, like the outbox pattern.
  • Rebalancing: moving data when adding shards, without downtime.
  • Unique IDs: auto-increment per shard collides, so use UUIDs or an ID generator.

That's why sharding is the last step, after caching, query tuning, a bigger machine and read replicas.

Replication vs Sharding

Question Replication Sharding
Each machine holds All the data Part of the data
More read capacity Yes Yes
More write capacity No Yes
Survives a machine failure Yes Only with replication
Complexity Moderate High

Large systems use both: each shard is a small primary with its replicas.

The Answer in Short

  1. Replication copies all data to replicas: more reads, safety, and nearby copies, but not more writes.
  2. Asynchronous replicas lag; read your own writes from the primary after a change.
  3. Sharding splits data across databases: more writes and storage, but harder queries, joins and transactions.
  4. Choose a shard key that spreads load evenly and keeps data read together on one shard.
  5. Shard last, after caching, tuning, scaling up and replicas.
